column2: Then the god Mahadeva, trident in hand, destroyer of Bhaga's eyes, taking the sword, bright as the fire of the sun at the end of time,
and raising a three-peaked shield, like a cloud with lightning, moved in many ways, of great strength and prowess, brandishing the sword in the sky with the wish to end the Danavas.
As he roared his roar and let out loud laughter, the form of Rudra then became terrifying, Bharata.
Hearing of Rudra in that form, wishing to do dreadful deeds, all the Danavas, delighted, rushed upon him.
They rained stones and blazing brands, and other fearsome weapons, sharp-edged, iron-faced.
Then that army of the Danavas, shaken by the force of Rudra's sword, with its unfallen leader, wavered and was bewildered.
Wondrously, because of his speed, the asuras all took the one sword-bearer as a thousand as he moved.
Cutting, splitting, breaking, hewing, tearing and crushing, Rudra moved among the hosts of Daityas like fire in dry grass.
Broken by the force of the sword, their arms, thighs and chests cut, their heads sliced off, the great asuras fell on the ground.
Other Danavas, broken and pressed by Rudra's blows, crying out to one another, fled in all directions.
Some entered the earth, others the mountains; others went to the sky, others entered the waters.
In that great and exceedingly dreadful battle, the earth then looked terrifying, a mire of blood.
Strewn, mighty-armed, with the huge bodies of the Danavas drenched in blood, it seemed like mountains with kimshuka trees.
Soaked with blood, the earth then shone, dark, like a woman bewildered with intoxication, her garment wet with red.
Having slain the Danavas and made the world uplifted by dharma, Rudra quickly put off his dreadful form and the Auspicious One took an auspicious form.
Then all the great sages and all the hosts of gods honoured the god of gods with a wondrous victory.
Then the blessed Rudra, honouring Vishnu, gave him the sword, wet with Danava blood, the guardian of dharma.
Vishnu gave it to Marichi, and the blessed Marichi to the great sages; the sages gave the sword to Vasava.
Mahendra gave it to the guardians of the world, and the guardians, son, gave the great sword to Manu, son of the Sun.
And they said to him, "Be lord of men from now; protect the subjects with the sword whose womb is dharma.
Those who have transgressed the bridge of dharma, for subtle or gross reasons, should be guarded by assigning punishment according to dharma, not at will.
Restraint by harsh words is punishment, and also fines rich in gold; maiming of the body, or death, for no small cause.
These forms of the sword, beginning with harsh words, should be directed; for the sword's measures arise from exceeding the measure."
Then, installing his own son as lord of the subjects, Manu gave the sword to Kshupa for the protection of the people.
From Kshupa Ikshvaku took it, from Ikshvaku Pururavas, from him Ayu got it, and then Nahusha on earth.
Yayati from Nahusha, Puru from him; from him Amurtarayas got it, and then King Bhumishaya.
Bharata, son of Dushyanta, got the sword from Bhumishaya, and from him the knower of dharma Aidabida, king.
Then from Aidabida Dhundhumara, lord of men, got it; from Dhundhumara Kambhoja, and from him Muchukunda.
From Muchukunda Marutta, from Marutta Raivata, from Raivata Yuvanashva, and from Yuvanashva Raghu.
Born in the line of Ikshvaku, the mighty Harinashva came after him; from Harinashva Shunaka got the sword, and then from Shunaka
the righteous-souled Ushinara; from him the Bhojas and Yadavas; from the Yadus Shibi got it, and from Shibi Pratardana.
From Pratardana Ashtaka, from Ashtaka Rushadashva, from Rushadashva Bharadvaja, then Drona, then Kripa; and from him you, with your brothers, have obtained the supreme sword.
Its constellation is the Krittikas, its deity Agni, its lineage the Rohinis, and its highest teacher Rudra.
Learn from me, Pandava, the eight secret names of the sword, by reciting which one always wins victory.
Asi, Vishasana, Khadga, Tikshnavartma, Durasada, Shrigarbha, Vijaya, and Dharmapala.
The sword is foremost among weapons, son of Madri; it was fashioned by Maheshvara, as the Purana has settled.
Prithu produced the first bow, scourge of foes; by it this earth was formerly protected by Vena's son.
This is the sages' account, son of Madri; you should take it as authority; and the sword should always be honoured by those skilled in war.
Thus the first account has been related to you at length, bull of the Bharatas: the origin of the sword and its transmission, as it was.
Having heard here the supreme means of the sword in every way, a man gains fame and attains the endless hereafter.
[Yudhishthira said:] "The conduct of the world rests on dharma, wealth and desire; which of these is the greatest, which the middle, and which the least?
And in which should one restrain oneself in order to conquer the three aims? You who are content should be able to speak the settled word as it is."
Then Vidura, knower of the truth of the course of wealth, first, quick of wit, spoke, remembering the dharmashastra.
Much learning, austerity, renunciation, faith, sacrificial action, forbearance, purity of heart, compassion, truth and self-restraint are the wealth of the self.
Hold to this alone; let your mind not waver; for dharma and wealth have this as their root; this is the one word of benefit.
By dharma alone the sages crossed over; on dharma the worlds are founded; by dharma the gods dwell in heaven; in dharma wealth is established.
Dharma, king, is best in virtue, wealth is called the middle, and desire the least, so say the wise; therefore one should be intent on dharma, with a controlled self.
When he had finished speaking, Partha, skilled in the science of wealth and knowing the truth of what was said, spoke without weariness.
For the victorious man of wealth is able to worship the highest dharma and also to pursue desire, which is hard to get for those who have not mastered themselves.
Dharma and desire are parts of wealth, so the tradition says; by the success of wealth both of these will be achieved.
Beings of higher birth constantly wait upon a man whose wealth has arisen, as upon Brahma.
Wearing matted locks and deerskins, self-controlled, smeared with mud, masters of their senses, shaven and without thread, they live apart, seeking wealth.
Others wear ochre robes, bearded and modest, learned and calm, freed from all possessions.
Some seek wealth, others desire heaven, some return to their families, each following his own path.
Believers and unbelievers, restrained, intent on restraint; ignorance is darkness become, knowledge is light.
He who unites servants with enjoyments and enemies with punishments is the man of wealth. This is my view, best of the intelligent, as it is; now learn the word of these two, whose speech is bound.
Then the two sons of Madri, skilled in dharma and wealth, Nakula and Sahadeva, spoke the highest word.
Sitting and lying, moving and standing, one should make a firm effort for wealth, by various means, high and low.
When this is well established, hard to get and most dear, one gains desires here visibly; there is no doubt.
Wealth joined with dharma and dharma joined with wealth are like honey joined with nectar; therefore both are held good here.
One without wealth has no desire; so how can the unrighteous man have wealth? Therefore the world is alarmed at one cast out from dharma and wealth.
Therefore wealth should be won by a controlled man with dharma first; and among trusting beings everything is possible.
One should practise dharma first, then wealth joined with dharma, and then desire afterward, for that is the fruit for one whose purpose is accomplished.
Having said these words, the two sons of the Ashvins fell silent, and Bhimasena then began to speak.
One without desire does not desire wealth, one without desire does not wish for dharma, and there is no one who desires without desire; therefore desire excels.
Sages joined with desire are intent on austerity, living on palasha fruits and roots, feeding on air, well restrained.
Others are devoted to the Vedic discussions, masters of study, in shraddha, sacrificial rites, giving and receiving.
Merchants, farmers, herdsmen, craftsmen, artisans and those who perform rites for the gods are engaged in their tasks by desire.
Others enter the ocean, men joined with desire; for desire is of many forms; all is continually by desire.
There is no being, nor has there been, nor will there be, beyond what has desire as its self; this is the essence, great king; dharma and wealth rest on it.
As butter comes from curds, so desire comes from wealth and dharma; oil is better than oil-cake, ghee better than whey,
flower and fruit are better than the wood; desire is the best of dharma and wealth; as the juice of flowers is honey, so happiness is born of desire.
Delight in women, beautifully adorned, intoxicated, speaking sweetly; come to them, enjoy desire, for desire, king, strikes with speed.
This is my view, standing in this assembly; let there be no doubt about it, son of Dharma; the word of the good, joined, of no slight substance, with great gentleness, has been uttered.
Dharma, wealth and desire should be served equally; but the man who serves only one is the lowest. They say the one who serves two is middling, and the best is he who delights in the three.
The wise, anointed with sandal paste, adorned with varied garlands and ornaments, having spoken in brief and in detail, Bhima, the youngest, ceased.
Then, after a moment, Dharmaraja, the much-learned, best of those who uphold dharma, having thought over their words well, spoke smiling, in truthful speech.

Without doubt you all have settled the dharmashastras and know the authorities; I wished to know, and what you said as the final word I have heard. But hear now my word too, with undivided minds.
mahabharata:12:161.42	The man who is attached neither to sin nor to merit, nor to wealth, dharma or desire, freed from faults, to whom clod and gold are equal, is freed from the accomplishments of pain and pleasure.
mahabharata:12:161.43	Beings are bound with birth and death, joined with the changes of age, and again awakened by those and those; they praise liberation, and we do not know it.
mahabharata:12:161.44	For the awakened, these do not exist through affection": so the blessed Self-born said, and the wise who are intent on nirvana say it; therefore one should make neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant.
This is the chief thing, not acting at will; I act as I am appointed; destiny appoints all beings; know that destiny is stronger.

One does not gain by action what is not to be gained; know that whatever is to be, all comes to be; even one lacking the three aims finds wealth; therefore this is a secret for the good of the world."
Then, having understood that whole speech, the best, in tune with their minds and very reasoned, they cheered and rejoiced, and made folded hands to the hero of the Kurus.

Hearing that speech of Partha, adorned with lovely letters and sounds, pleasing to the mind, with the thorns of its words removed, the kings praised it; and again, undiminished in spirit, he asked the son of the best of rivers about the highest dharma.
[Yudhishthira said:] "What sort of men are gentle, and by whom is the highest affection gained? Who are patient in the future and in the present? Tell me of them.
For there is neither abundant wealth nor are there relatives and kin where friends stand; so I think, friends stand.
For a friend who will listen is hard to find, and a friend who does good is hard to find; best of those who uphold dharma, you should explain all this."
[Bhishma said:] "Learn from me in full, Yudhishthira, as I tell it, the men with whom, king, one may and may not make an alliance, in truth.
The greedy, cruel, one who has given up dharma, the deceitful, the crafty, the petty, of sinful conduct, suspicious of all, and lazy,
the procrastinator, the crooked, the harsh, the violator of the teacher's wife, one who abandons in misfortune, evil-souled, shameless,
the one who sees sin everywhere, the unbeliever, the reviler of the Veda, he whose senses are scattered, who roams in the world devoted to desire,
the untruthful, the hated by the world, the unsteady in agreement, the backbiter, the unlearned, the envious, of sinful resolve,
and the dull-witted who is not content, though one carries on as far as able, and who treats a friend ever as a foe, bull among men,
he who is angry at the wrong time and suddenly estranged, who quickly abandons good friends, the sinner,
the fool who, over a small wrong or one done through ignorance, serves only his task among friends, a hater of friends, king,
the enemy with a friend's face, who looks with crooked eye and covets, who is not pleased by good: such a man one should abandon.
The drunkard, the hater, the cruel, the pitiless and harsh, the tormentor of others, the betrayer of friends, the one intent on killing creatures,
the ungrateful, the lowest in the world, are in no way to be allied with, nor the fault-finder; hear now whom you may ally with.
Those of good family, eloquent, skilled in knowledge and discernment, knowers of friends, grateful, all-knowing, free of grief,
endowed with sweetness, true to their word, masters of their senses, given to exercise, maintaining sons, of high lineage,
handsome, virtuous, not greedy, who have conquered fatigue, free of famed faults: these a king should accept.
The good are content, lord, with conduct as far as they are able; they are not angry out of place and not estranged without cause.
Estranged, they are not angry, even in mind, skilled in affairs; devoted to a friend's business even at cost to themselves, they do not turn from friends, like a dyed woollen cloth.
They do not show their friends faults such as greed and delusion in affairs and with women; trusted, affectionate to kin,

for whom wealth is like clod and gold, honest in mind toward friends, who move about without pride, with their wealth and ornaments freely given, supporting their dependants, ever devoted to their master's interest,
the king who makes an alliance with such best of men has his kingdom spread, like the moonlight of the lord of the stars.
Constant in the shastras, with anger conquered, strong, fond of battle, patient, endowed with virtue and character: such best of men are fit for alliance.
And of those men joined with faults whom I have named, sinless one, the lowest, king, the ungrateful, the killer of friends, is to be abandoned, the evil-doer, by all; this is certain."
[Yudhishthira said:] "I wish to hear at length the matter, king; tell me of the betrayer of friends and the ungrateful man, of whom you have spoken."
[Bhishma said:] "Well, I shall relate an ancient tale of what took place in the northern region among the barbarians, lord of men.
A brahmana of the middle country, dark-limbed, who had given up Brahman, seeing a village crowded with people, entered it, wishing alms.
There was a robber there, rich, knowing the distinctions of all classes, devoted to brahmanas, true to his word, and devoted to giving.
Going to his house he asked for alms, and for a lodging for dwelling, and for alms for the rainy season.
He gave that brahmana a new garment of fitting kind, and a woman too, past her youth, then without a husband.
Receiving all this from the robber, the brahmana, glad at heart, Gautama, took his pleasure with her in that excellent house, king.
He also gave help to the robber in his family affairs; he lived there for years in the prosperous village of the Shabaras, and Gautama made great effort in shooting arrows.
Gautama killed daily crooked-limbed creatures, all within the range of his arrows, king, as did the bands of robbers.
Devoted to violence, without compassion, ever intent on killing creatures, Gautama by nearness became equal to the robbers.
Living thus happily in the robber village then, many months went by as he killed many birds.
Then once another twice-born came to that place, matted-haired, wearing bark and deerskin, devoted to study, pure,
humble, of restrained diet, devoted to brahmanas, a master of the Veda, a celibate student from that country, a very dear friend of his; he came to the robber village where Gautama was.
Seeking a brahmana's house and avoiding shudra food, he roamed in every direction in the village crowded with robbers.
Then that best of the twice-born entered Gautama's house, and Gautama too having arrived, the two met each other.
Carrying a load of crooked-limbed birds, bow in hand, guilty, his body drenched in blood, he had reached the door of his house.
Seeing him like an ogre, ruined, fallen from his state, the brahmana recognised him, felt shame, and said:

What are you doing here out of folly? You are a brahmana, born in a good family, known in the middle country; how have you come to be a robber?
mahabharata:12:162.45	Remember those foremost twice-born, famed masters of the Veda, in whose line you were born, such a defiler of the family.
mahabharata:12:162.46	Awake to yourself by yourself; remembering truth, character, learning, self-control and compassion, leave this dwelling, brahmana.
Thus addressed by his friend, wishing his good, he answered then, king, as if distressed, having made up his mind.

I am poor, best of the twice-born, and I know no Veda; know that I came here for a livelihood, best of brahmanas.
mahabharata:12:162.49	But by seeing you, brahmana sage, I know my purpose is achieved; we shall go together; stay here tonight, tomorrow.
Then he saw sea-going merchants standing on the road; he went with that caravan toward the ocean.
But that caravan, great king, in a mountain cave, was almost wholly destroyed by a rutting elephant.
Somehow the brahmana escaped from that caravan, fleeing in all directions for his life, and ran toward the north.
Separated from the caravan, from the place and from his goods, alone he ran through the forest like a kimpurusha.
Reaching a road toward the sea, he came upon a lovely great forest of flowering trees.
It was adorned with blossoming mango groves of all seasons, like a place in Nandana, frequented by yakshas and kinnaras.
It was adorned with groves of sal, palm, dhava and pipal trees, aloe, and the best sandal trees, on lovely, auspicious, fragrant mountain slopes.
On all sides, best of the twice-born, birds sang sweetly there; others with human faces, known as bharundas, and bhulinga birds were everywhere toward the sea.
He saw a great banyan tree, round, graced with splendour, adorned with matching branches like a parasol.
Its root was well sprinkled with fine sandal water, endowed with divine flowers, beautiful, like the Grandfather's seat.
Seeing it, Gautama was pleased, an unsurpassed place beloved of sages, holy, like a temple of the gods, surrounded by flowering trees; coming to it with joy, he sat beneath it.
As Gautama sat there, Kauravya, a pleasant, auspicious, pure breeze blew, touching the flowers, delighting all Gautama's limbs, king.
That brahmana, tired, touched by the holy wind, found comfort and slept; and the sun went down.
Then, when the sun had set and twilight had come, the best of birds returned to his dwelling from the world of Brahma.
He was known as Nadijangha, dear friend of Brahma, king of cranes, greatly wise, born of Kashyapa himself.
Famed as Rajadharma, he was unequalled on earth, the son of a divine maiden, splendid, learned, bright as the lord of the gods.
Covered with polished gold, with ornaments like the sun, adorned in all limbs, god-born, he blazed with splendour.
Seeing the twice-born arrived, Gautama was astonished; his mind seized by hunger and thirst, he looked on him also with a wish to kill.
[Rajadharma said:] "Welcome to you, brahmana; by good fortune you have come to my house; the sun has set and this twilight has arrived.
You have come to my dwelling, a dear and blameless guest; honoured, you shall go in the morning, with the rite seen in scripture."
[Rajadharma said:] "Sir, I am a son of Kashyapa, and my mother is Dakshayani; you are a guest endowed with virtue; welcome to you, best of brahmanas."
[Bhishma said:] Having given him honour by the rite seen in scripture, he prepared a divine seat made of sal flowers.
He also provided for him large fish that roam in the regions crossed by Bhagiratha's chariot and served by the Ganga.
The Kashyapa offered to Gautama, the guest, a well-kindled fire and plump fish.
When the brahmana had eaten and was content, the great-minded one fanned him with his wings to remove his weariness.
Then, as he sat rested, he asked about his lineage; he said "Gautama," and the brahmana told nothing else.
He gave him a divine bed of leaves, scented with divine flowers and rich in fragrance; and he slept there happily.
Then, as Gautama sat on the bed, the king of cranes, the eloquent Kashyapa, asked him, "What is the reason for your coming?"
I appear before you as your friend, and you are my well-wisher; so I shall strive that you become a man of wealth.
Then at dawn, having inquired after his comfort, he said, "Go, gentle one, by this road, and you will have your purpose done.
Three yojanas from here lives the great lord of the rakshasas, famed as Virupaksha, my mighty friend.
Go to him, best of the twice-born, urged by my word; he will give you the desires you wish; there is no doubt."
Thus addressed, Gautama set out, king, free of weariness, eating fruits like nectar as he wished.
On that road, great king, he went quickly, enjoying groves of sandal and aloe and of bark and leaf trees.
Then he reached a city named Merusvraja, with mountain gateways, mountain ramparts and bulwarks, and mountain engines and bars.
It was made known to that wise lord of the rakshasas, king, that a dear guest had been sent by a friend with affection.
Then that lord of the rakshasas said to his servants, Yudhishthira, "Let Gautama be brought quickly from the city gate."
Then men in white turbans came from that excellent city, calling out "Gautama!" and reached the city gate.
They said to him, great king, "We are sent by the lord of the rakshasas; hurry, come quickly; the king wishes to see you.
The hero, lord of the rakshasas, famed as Virupaksha, is eager to see you; so let it be arranged quickly."
Then the brahmana rushed forward, free of weariness from astonishment, Gautama, seeing the splendour of that city, greatly amazed.
With those same men he hastened to the king's house, wishing to see the lord of the rakshasas.
He was asked his lineage, conduct, study and celibate studentship; but the brahmana said nothing there but his lineage name.
Seeing him devoid of Vedic lustre and without study, knowing only his gotra, the king asked about his dwelling.
Where is your dwelling, good sir, what is your lineage, and is your wife a brahmana? Tell me the truth; do not be afraid; rest at ease.
[Gautama said:] "I was born in the middle country; my dwelling is in a village of Shabaras; my wife is a shudra, a remarried widow; this I tell you truly."
[Bhishma said:] Then the king considered, "How should this be done? How can I do good?" so he thought in his mind.

This brahmana is by birth the friend of that great-souled one, and he has been sent to me by Kashyapa.
mahabharata:12:165.8	I shall do what pleases him, for he has always relied on me; he is my brother, my kinsman, a friend dear to my heart.
mahabharata:12:165.9	Today, on the full moon of Kartika, a thousand excellent brahmanas will eat with me; he too will eat among them, and wealth shall be given to him.
By the command of the lord of the rakshasas, seats were laid for them, best of the Bharatas, spread by the servants on the ground with fine carpets.
On them the king honoured the best of the twice-born as they sat, and they shone, great king, like lords of the constellations.
Then he gave the brahmanas golden dishes marked with diamonds, spotless and auspicious, filled with excellent food and dipped in honey and ghee.
Each day, at Ashadha and Magha, many brahmanas obtain from him the excellent meal they wish, always honoured.
But especially on Kartika he gives to the brahmanas: at the end of autumn, on the full moon, jewels, so it is heard.
Gold, silver, gems and pearls, great diamonds, and cat's-eyes and woollen deerskins,
piling heaps of jewels for the fees, Bharata, the renowned Virupaksha then said to the best of the twice-born:
Take these jewels as you wish, according to your zeal. And in whatever vessels you have eaten, best of the twice-born, take those very ones and go to your homes, Bharata.
When the great-souled lord of the rakshasas had spoken thus, the bulls among brahmanas took those jewels as they wished.
Then all those brahmanas, honoured with precious auspicious jewels, in clean garments, became well pleased.
Then the lord of the rakshasas again spoke to the twice-born, having stopped the rakshasas who had come from various directions:
For one day, brahmanas, you have no fear anywhere from rakshasas; rejoice; go as you wish; do not delay.
Then all the groups of brahmanas fled on every side; and Gautama too, taking a load of gold in haste,
carrying it with difficulty, hero, came to the banyan; he sat down, exhausted, tired and hungry.
Then, king, the best of birds, Rajadharma, came to him, and greeted Gautama with welcome, affectionate as a friend.
The bird removed his weariness with strokes of the tips of his wings, and the wise one honoured him and prepared a meal.
Having eaten and rested well, Gautama then thought: "This load of fine gold has been taken by me through greed and delusion, and my way is long.
There is nothing to eat on the road to sustain my life; what shall I do to keep myself alive?" so he thought.
[Bhishma said:] "Ikshvaku, king, was the son of Manu Prajapati; to that king, radiant as the sun, a hundred sons were born.
Then the goldsmiths, whose number cannot be reckoned, made bowls, dishes, jars and seats.
There, living on air or fasting, with this wife of mine, hero, I shall practise the highest austerity.
Seeing Shaineya and his son slain, the delight of the Yadus, Keshava in anger seized a handful of eraka reeds.
[Dharma said:] "Long ago, son, you were tested by me at the Dvaita forest, where your brothers were slain when they ventured to fetch water.
The iron cauldrons and the dreadful stones were no longer seen; and the deformed bodies that King Kaunteya had seen all around there became invisible.
